value.overview: The Blackpoll Warbler is a long-distance migratory songbird of the boreal forests of North America. It breeds mainly across Alaska and Canada and winters mostly in northern South America. Its migration includes one of the most remarkable nonstop ocean crossings known among songbirds. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon to rare visitor, recorded mainly during migration and occasionally in the nonbreeding season. It is usually encountered singly in forested areas, woodland edges, and other suitable cover.
value.classification: The Blackpoll Warbler is a member of the New World warbler family, Parulidae, and the genus Setophaga. Its scientific name is Setophaga striata.
value.identification: This small warbler has a short tail, thin bill, pointed wings, and distinctive orange-yellow legs. In breeding plumage, the male has a black cap, white cheeks, black facial markings, and heavy black streaking on the back and sides. Females are paler and more finely streaked. Birds seen in migration or winter are much duller, with olive or yellow-green upperparts, pale yellow underparts, dark streaking, a dark eyeline, and two white wingbars. The legs remain a useful field mark.
value.rangeHabitat: Blackpoll Warblers breed mainly in spruce, tamarack, and other coniferous forests across northern North America, including boreal and subarctic regions. During migration they use mature and second-growth evergreen or deciduous forest, woodland edges, scrub, parks, and gardens. The species winters primarily in northern South America. In Costa Rica it is a scarce and irregular visitor rather than a common wintering warbler; documented records indicate that individuals may occur during passage or remain temporarily in forested and wooded habitats, especially where migrant cover and food are available.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Most birds move south in autumn toward northern South America, often crossing the Atlantic or Caribbean from eastern North America. Spring migration is generally more gradual through the Caribbean and eastern North America. In Costa Rica, the Blackpoll Warbler is rare or uncommon, with occasional records during migration and possibly in the nonbreeding season; it does not breed there.
value.breeding: Blackpoll Warblers usually breed in low, open coniferous forest, especially spruce and tamarack stands, and may also nest in alder or willow thickets near the northern treeline. The female builds a cup-shaped nest, usually placed in a conifer or shrub, and lays a small clutch of pale eggs marked with darker spots. Both parents feed the nestlings. Breeding occurs during the short northern summer, when insect abundance is greatest.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of insects and other small arthropods, including caterpillars, beetles, flies, aphids, ants, and spiders. During migration and winter, the species may also consume berries and other small fruits when insects are scarce. It usually forages actively among leaves and small branches, picking prey from foliage. It may search near the trunks of conifers on breeding grounds and often feeds in mixed-species flocks during migration.
value.behavior: Blackpoll Warblers are active, restless foragers that move through foliage while searching for small prey. They are often difficult to see because they remain among leaves and branches, although their bright legs and wingbars can be noticeable. Males sing on the breeding grounds with a high, rapid, evenly pitched series of notes. Outside the breeding season they are generally quiet. Their autumn migration is especially notable for long over-water flights, sometimes lasting several days.

conservation.populationTrend: Declining. Long-term monitoring indicates substantial population losses across parts of its range, although the species is still widespread.
conservation.threats: Major concerns include habitat loss and degradation in boreal breeding forests and in South American wintering areas. Climate change may alter northern forest conditions and the timing or availability of food. During migration, collisions with illuminated buildings, towers, and other structures can kill large numbers of birds. Severe weather during long ocean crossings may also increase mortality.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore boreal forests, migration stopover sites, and South American wintering habitat. Reduce unnecessary outdoor lighting during migration, especially near windows and tall structures, and use bird-safe window treatments. Support conservation programs that monitor migratory birds and promote sustainable forestry. In Costa Rica, protecting forest patches, wooded corridors, and other stopover habitat can benefit this and many other migrant species.
